Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Explain the fundamentals of radiation therapy.
List the indications and contraindications to radiation therapy for the management of bone
sarcoma.
Discuss the administration of radiation therapy for the management of bone sarcoma.
Identify complications of radiation therapy.
Introduction
Radiation therapy is part of the multimodal management of sarcoma, complementing systemic
therapy (eg, chemotherapy) and surgical management.
It is an integral component in the management of high-grade soft-tissue sarcoma; however, its
role is somewhat limited in bone sarcoma.

Radiation Therapy Basic Knowledge
Mechanism of action is direct damage to DNA and the creation of free radicals.
Integral role in soft-tissue sarcoma management
Used for radiosensitive bone sarcomas
Two major types of radiation therapy
Photons (x-rays)
Protons (particle therapy)

Radiation Therapy Basic Knowledge
Radiation therapy works by directly damaging DNA or by indirectly creating free radicals1
(Figure 1). It is integral in the management of high-grade soft-tissue sarcoma; however,
its role in bone sarcoma is mostly limited to sarcomas that are radiosensitive. Radiation
therapy is nondiscriminatory in its effect on the tissue and, therefore, must be directed
to the specific target (ie, sarcoma) to avoid unnecessary damage to normal tissue. Two
major types of radiation therapy are used: photons (x-rays) and protons (particle
therapy). For a general overview of radiation therapy, review Resources 1 and 2.2

Figure 1 Illustration shows the direct and indirect action of photons on the DNA
structure. In the indirect mechanism, an electron dislodged by a photon ionizes a water
molecule to produce a free radical, which will damage the DNA. In the direct mechanism,
a dislodged electron directly causes damage to the DNA structure. (Reproduced from
Gross CE, Frank RM, Hsu AR, Diaz A, Gitelis S: External beam radiation therapy for
orthopaedic pathology. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2015;23[4]:243-252.)
Indications
Limited role in the primary management of bone sarcoma
Ewing sarcoma: with curative intent, if surgical morbidity is excessive
Other sensitive tumors: solitary plasmacytoma, chordoma, hemangioendothelioma
Unresectable bone sarcoma or positive margin resection
Recurrent or metastatic disease not amenable to resection


Indications
Radiation therapy is well described in the management of Ewing sarcoma and is a local
control option for this pathology.3,4 Local control via radiation therapy may exceed 65%
and usually is improved further if surgical resection can be performed (90% to 95% local
control).4 The results are observed in patients with isolated pelvic Ewing sarcoma, with
local control via radiation therapy (and chemotherapy) ranging from 67% to 83% in a
large study.5 With respect to overall survival, the rate is substantially improved if surgical
management can be performed.5,6
Other bone tumors that are sensitive to radiation therapy include solitary
plasmacytoma, chordoma, and hemangioendothelioma.7 Radiation therapy often is used
for sarcomas that are deemed unresectable (or unresectable with appropriate margins),
in patients in whom surgical morbidity is too high, or in recurrent or positive-margin
disease scenarios in which surgical excision may not be feasible.
Contraindications
Sarcomas resistant to radiation therapy that are amenable to resection
Osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma
Young patients, because of the risk of secondary sarcoma

Contraindications
Conventional high-grade osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma generally are regarded as
radioresistant, and the routine use of radiation therapy is relatively contraindicated;
however, in some circumstances, high-dose radiation therapy has been used
successfully with curative intent.8-10 Proton therapy also has shown some promise in the
curative management of chondrosarcoma in particular;11,12 however, in most patients in
whom limb salvage surgery can be achieved with acceptable morbidity, radiation therapy

Technique
Treatment Planning
Gross tumor volume14: actual tumor visualized on imaging studies (Figures 2 and 3)
Clinical target volume14: additional margin around the gross tumor volume, accounting for
unobserved microscopic disease
Planning target volume14: additional margin around the clinical target volume to ensure the
entirety of the gross tumor volume and the clinical target volume are managed via the planned
dose of radiation therapy

Type of radiation therapy used
Photons: traditional x-rays
Pass through the body, affecting all tissues in their path
Particle therapy: most commonly protons
Deliver energy at a planned depth/location
Patient Positioning
Custom molds (eg, bean bag) typically are used to ensure the patient is in the same position
for each treatment.
Patient positioning varies based on anatomic location affected and nearby at-risk structures
nearby.
Typical Dosing/Regimen

Radiation therapy typically is delivered in fractions (small doses over time) to reduce the risk of
complications (eg, 2 gray [Gy] daily for 25 days = 50 Gy treatment)
Ewing sarcoma: 45 Gy15
Chordoma (unresectable): greater than 70 Gy15
Chondrosarcoma: none for resectable disease; greater than 70 Gy for unresectable or gross
positive margin15
Osteosarcoma: none for resectable disease; greater than 60 Gy for unresectable or gross
positive margin15

Typical Dosing/Regimen
Planning for radiation therapy for bone sarcoma (or soft-tissue sarcoma) must consider
the visible disease and the presumed microscopic disease extending from the gross
tumor. The planned radiation therapy field considers these factors and factors such as
nearby critical structures at risk (eg, neurovascular structures) and the best position for
the patient. Patient positioning is particularly important for photon radiation (x-rays)
because the irradiation passes completely through the treated body part, potentially
exposing normal tissue. Proton therapy allows for more focused treatment but is less
commonly used because of its expense and the need for a specialized facility and
because photons usually can be delivered safely in extremity locations in which most
bone sarcomas occur. Radiation therapy doses vary by pathology, with more sensitive
tumors requiring less radiation therapy (eg, 45 Gy for Ewing sarcoma) and resistant
tumors (osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, chordoma) requiring doses as high as 70 Gy.15
To avoid the risk of complication from such high doses, radiation therapy typically is
delivered in small fractions over time. Considerable variation exists, and a radiation
oncologist ultimately decides the best treatment regimen for each patient.
Complications/Adverse Effects
Fatigue
Pain
Soft-tissue reaction

Wound healing complications
Stiffness
Osteopenia/osteoporosis
Fracture
Neural injury/nerve palsy
Secondary sarcoma (late)
Other secondary cancers

Complications/Adverse Effects
Common adverse effects of radiation therapy include fatigue, pain, and soft-tissue
reaction (redness, peeling, blisters). Additional adverse effects include
stiffness/arthrofibrosis, wound healing complications (eg, delayed healing, wound
dehiscence, infection); soft-tissue damage to critical structures (eg, nerve injury); and
focal osteopenia/osteoporosis, which may lead to pathologic fracture.13 Radiation-
induced sarcoma is a devastating complication that may occur many years after initial
radiation therapy, with the histology being different than the original tumor (eg, post-
radiation osteosarcoma developing decades after treatment of Ewing sarcoma; (Figure
4). Radiation therapy also may lead to other secondary cancers; therefore, long-term
screening is prudent13,16-22 (Table 1; Resource 3).
Figure 4 AP radiographs of the pelvis of a young man with a solitary plasmacytoma. A,
Radiograph obtained years after radiation therapy for the management of the solitary
plasmacytoma shows osteosarcoma involving the right periacetabular region. B,
Radiograph demonstrates complete hemipelvectomy to achieve negative margins.

Summary
Radiation therapy is an important modality occasionally used in the management of primary
bone sarcoma, particularly Ewing sarcoma.
Currently, radiation therapy has a very limited role in the management of osteosarcoma and
chondrosarcoma because these tumors are radioresistant.
Radiation therapy typically is avoided if negative-margin surgical management is achievable,
particularly in younger patients, because of the risk of secondary sarcoma later in life.
Radiation therapy is particularly effective in patients with unresectable disease and recurrent
local disease, and if surgical margins are unacceptable.
